scenarios.answer:
At a high level, EKOS is a compiler pipeline. Its core compiler infrastructure (ekos-compiler-core) provides the PassManager, Scheduler, Diagnostics, and Config. Enterprise systems are ingested through observer plugins built on the Observer trait and connector contract in ekos-observation-sdk — including Git (ekos-plugin-git), Pentaho Kettle (ekos-plugin-pentaho), file system (ekos-plugin-file), Rust (ekos-plugin-rust), Elixir (ekos-plugin-elixir), ClickHouse (ekos-plugin-clickhouse), local documents (ekos-plugin-localdocs), crypto entities (ekos-plugin-crypto), Confluence (ekos-plugin-confluence), GitHub (ekos-plugin-github), JavaScript/TypeScript (ekos-plugin-javascript), and Python (ekos-plugin-python).

The compiled representation flows through a Knowledge Intermediate Representation (KIR) with four canonical node types (ekos-kir), and the semantic compiler pass compiles KIR into a Canonical Knowledge Model (Phase 8) (ekos-semantic). That compiled output is persisted in an append-only semantic knowledge ledger with a SQLite backend (ekos-ledger), and ekos-runtime provides read-only state reconstruction from that ledger.

Supporting structure includes the Enterprise Knowledge Language parser/interpreter (ekos-ekl), identity resolution that merges synonymous concepts (ekos-identity), knowledge recovery compiler passes (SqlAnalyzer, GitAnalyzer, LLM integration) (ekos-recovery), generated documentation rendering compiled ledger objects as Markdown/HTML/diagrams (ekos-docs-gen), Pentaho-to-dbt model export (ekos-dbt-gen), distributed-mode coordination and storage (ekos-cluster, ekos-distributed, ekos-segment-backend), a deterministic simulation engine (ekos-simulation), a marketing agent (ekos-marketing), and a live NL-to-SQL query engine over compiled ClickHouse schemas (ekos-clickhouse-query).

scenarios.answer: The Semantic Knowledge Ledger is the EKOS component specified in RFC 0004 (accepted, retroactively documented; built from around 2026-07-04 and already assumed by RFC 0005). It serves as the ledger/knowledge store: its design calls for atomicity, an indexed `get_object(id)` lookup rather than full-log scans, and a historical state index. The write path appends records and threads a real `ArtifactId` through append call sites. Backend evolution since that design is documented, and `PartitionedLedger` is implemented as a drop-in `KnowledgeStore` per RFC 0111 amendment 2026-08-29 §4, with `PartitionError` mapping to `LedgerError`.

scenarios.answer: The EKOS Runtime is read-only by design because it is the consumer API of EKOS: AI agents and CLI users go through the Runtime — never directly to the Ledger — and the Runtime has no `&mut self` methods that affect the ledger (RFC 0005). Its own description confirms this: "Read-only state reconstruction from the ledger" / "Read-only state reconstruction from the Semantic Knowledge Ledger." The write path is deliberately kept separate: reads go through the Runtime, while writes go directly through `&dyn KnowledgeStore` (the same access level `commit.rs` already has), leaving the Runtime itself read-only.

The SQL DDL recovery analyzer is implemented by the **`ekos_recovery`** crate — the recovery crate at `ekos/crates/recovery`. Its `src/sql_analyzer.rs` defines `SqlAnalyzerPass`, which extracts `KirObject`s (tables as entities) and `KirRelationship`s (FK edges) from SQL DDL, and exposes `parse_ddl_structural` (DDL → KIR, no LLM). The crate name is confirmed by the benchmark at `benchmark/benches/sql_analyzer.rs`, which calls `ekos_recovery::parse_ddl_structural`.

AiRuntime is a Rust struct defined at `ekos/crates/runtime/src/ai.rs:204` (source span lines 204–218). Its description states it answers natural-language questions grounded in the Knowledge Ledger via a pipeline: retrieve candidate objects with `Runtime::find_objects`, expand each into its neighbourhood with `Runtime::load_neighborhood`, ground the prompt with `Runtime::reconstruct_state` (object + relationships + evidence as JSON), then ask the LLM and parse a trailing citation block.

scenarios.answer: The crate is **`ekos-ekl`** (located at `ekos/crates/ekl`). Its Cargo.toml describes it as "Enterprise Knowledge Language: parser + interpreter (RFC 0010)", and it provides the parser (`ekl_parse`, producing an `EklAst`) and the interpreter (`EklInterpreter`, which compiles the AST to `Runtime` calls and evaluates predicates). The CLI command `ekos/crates/cli/src/commands/ekl.rs` uses `ekos_ekl::{EklInterpreter, ekl_parse, interpreter::default_returns}` to run EKL queries.

The claims do not use the exact phrase "Canonical Knowledge Model" or the word "primitives," but they do describe the fact model that conclusions rest on. A ledger entry payload decomposes into facts as `(entity, attribute, position, value)` tuples (RFC 0016 Phase 1, `ekos/crates/ledger/src/fact.rs`), and reasoning creates conclusions from evidence and facts (RFC 0065 section 8). So the four components that facts — and therefore conclusions built on facts — rest on are **entity, attribute, position, and value**. The claims do not explicitly state that these are the "four primitives" of a "Canonical Knowledge Model" or that every semantic conclusion rests on them.

The EKOS Runtime normally consumes knowledge only through the compiled ledger and never touches raw enterprise systems directly — that is the stated invariant: "AI systems consume knowledge through the Runtime only... they never touch raw enterprise systems directly." The Runtime is also described as read-only, reconstructing state from the ledger.

However, there is exactly one explicit, gated, audited exception: the ClickHouse connector, RFC 0056, implemented as `ekos_clickhouse_query` (crate `ekos/crates/clickhouse-query`). That path is a live NL-to-SQL query engine over a compiled ClickHouse schema, and it is described as "the first place that line gets crossed" — the one path in EKOS that crosses the invariant. It is audited and gated, and it enforces read-only behavior by rejecting anything but a single `SELECT` (with a `LIMIT max_rows` injected).

So: only the compiled ledger, with the single audited exception of the RFC 0056 ClickHouse live-query path.

The only "delete" mention in the claims is in a CLI branch command (`ekos/crates/cli/src/commands/branch.rs:104`), which is unrelated to ledger object deletion. So the claims support that the ledger's append-only design does not allow an object to be deleted once written — no delete capability for ledger objects is described.
